title: Ask for reviews that work
subtitle: Three small changes that get you detailed, recent reviews. No tricks, no paying for them.
intro: A row of five-star ratings with two words each tells a new customer very little. AI search looks at what reviews say and how recent they are, not just the star count. The good news: you don't need more customers to fix this. You need to ask a little differently.

callout.title: The one rule
callout.text: Never write reviews for customers, and never pay or reward them for one. Only ask. Everything in this guide is about asking better.

sections.title: Ask what you did
body: "Leave us a review" gets you a star and a few words. A specific question gets a specific answer.
bullets: "What did we help you with today? A sentence or two in a review would mean a lot."
people answer the question you ask. Ask about the job, and they'll describe the job.

sections.title: Ask the same week
body: Ask right after the job, while it's fresh. The customer still remembers the details, and recent reviews count.
bullets: when the customer says thank you, or when you hand over the finished work.
send your review link by text or email the same day, so it's one tap away.
a few reviews every month beats a burst once a year.

sections.title: Reply in plain words
body: Answer every review, good or bad, in a sentence or two. Thank the person and name the service you did.
bullets: "Thanks, Sam. Glad the boiler service went smoothly. See you next winter."
stay calm, say sorry for the trouble, and offer to sort it out directly.
it shows people a real, active business is behind the name.

playbook: Find your Google review link and save it on your phone.
Write your one question: "What did we help you with today?"
Ask every customer the same day the job is done.
Send the link by text or email right after you ask.
Reply to every new review within a few days, naming the service.
mistakes: Writing reviews yourself or asking friends to.
Offering a discount or gift in exchange for a review.
Asking weeks later, when the customer has forgotten the details.
Copy-paste replies that say the same thing every time.
Ignoring bad reviews instead of answering them calmly.
faq: Do I need hundreds of reviews?
No. Detailed, recent reviews from real customers matter more than a big number.
What if a customer writes a short review?
That's fine. Thank them anyway. The next question you ask will get a longer one.
sources: Reviews as trust signals for AI and local search (BrightLocal)
